text.p: Chiroscience Group Plc said on Friday it had gained a commercial edge over competitors in the quest for drugs to treat skin condition Psoriasis and bone-wasting disease osteoporosis.

In a telephone interview with Reuters, chief executive John Padfield said the addition last December of Seattle-based Darwin Discovery's skills in genetic research would greatly speed up the process of finding novel drugs.
"We can take gene targets and get into the clinic quickly," Padfield said.

Chiroscience acquired Seattle-based gene company Darwin Molecular in December for $113 million. On Friday it presented the early fruits of the combination of Darwin's biological skills and Chiroscience's own chemical-based approach to drug discovery to analysts in London. The company will make the same presentation in New York on Monday.
Drug companies increasingly believe understanding genetic building blocks will lead to the creation of drugs to provoke the body into defending itself from a whole range of illnesses.
Chiroscience said on Friday Darwin had already identified a possible gene linked to psoriasis which could lead to new drugs.

But Padfield said osteoporosis represented an even greater opportunity. "In the UK there are approximately two million sufferers of osteoporosis. In the U.S. there are around 22 million, and the healthcare cost is estimated to be $14 billion a year," he said.

He said Chiroscience's approach of trying to identify genes linked to loss of bone mass was in contrast to other research. "Most companies are focusing on preventing bone fracture. We are looking to actually increase bone density," he said.
The company said it expected a flow of news on the lead projects during the course of the year.

Padfield told Reuters Chiroscience was also in talks with several companies on licensing out Darwin's isolation of genes responsible for early-onset Alzheimer's Disease and the premature ageing disease known as Werner's Syndrome.

The company began the exploitation of Darwin's technical skills on Friday by announcing a collaboration with Hewlett-Packard Co on an automated gene analysis system which it said would greatly speed up the search for potential gene targets for drugs.
Padfield said the tie-up, which followed 18 months of work between Darwin and Hewlett-Packard, was a "fundamental leap forward in the way genes can be discovered".

He declined to give financial details of the accord but said it would benefit from Hewlett-Packard's marketing skills and showed the acquisition of Darwin "was not a blue sky merger," with revenues likely to flow in from the end of 1998.

David Galas, executive director of discovery research, told Reuters there were many potential uses for the system outside pharmaceuticals, including agricultural research. "We are not really sure how broadly the instrument will be applied but there are certainly a lot of opportunities," said Galas.

Padfield said Friday's announcements showed the merger was working. "This is delivering on promises," he said. "That was the thesis of the merger - to do things faster and better than other companies can at the moment."
